title: Feminist and womanist voices
hook: women theologians reread scripture and tradition, recovering women's voices

segments.voice: Yesterday, James Cone: the cross beside the lynching tree, and God on the side of the oppressed. Your line was the cross stands with them. Whose story did you carry yesterday? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-nine.

A servant woman runs into the desert. She's pregnant, she's been treated harshly, and she has nowhere to go. Her name is Hagar, an Egyptian in the household of Abraham and Sarah. By a spring of water in the wilderness, the angel of the Lord finds her and speaks to her by name. And then Hagar does something startling. She gives God a name: "Thou God seest me." Her story can be read as a side scene in Abraham's. Some theologians read it as the main one. Today, feminist and womanist voices.

Feminist theology is a name for rereading scripture and the Christian past with women in view. It asks: who is speaking here? Who is silent? Who got left out of the retelling? Scholars such as Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Rosemary Radford Ruether wrote in this way. Womanist theology grew from the experience of Black women, taking its name from a word used by the writer Alice Walker. One womanist theologian, Delores Williams, read Hagar as a mirror: a woman enslaved, used, and sent into the wilderness, and met there by God, who doesn't free her right away but helps her and her child survive. Read this way, women turn up at turning points in the story. In Mark, when the disciples have fled, women are watching the cross from a distance. In John, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus in the garden and goes to tell the disciples she has seen the Lord. Paul commends a woman he calls, in the King James spelling, Phebe, "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," and sends greetings to women who worked alongside him. None of this is hidden; it's on the page. Churches draw different conclusions from these texts, about leadership, ordination and roles. Some ordain women as pastors and priests; others hold that certain ministries belong to men. The method is open to anyone: read slowly, and ask whose story is also here.

Here's the practice: sit with one woman of the Bible. Settle, and breathe. Bring Hagar back to mind, alone by the spring in the wilderness. Notice what she's carrying: fear, exhaustion, a child on the way. Then hear a voice call her by name. And hear her answer, naming God as the one who sees her. Stay there with her. If you pray, you can speak to the God who sees. If you don't, notice who in your own life goes unseen. The bell holds the time.
Feminist and womanist voices. Women's rereadings of scripture and tradition, recovering stories like Hagar's, and the women at the cross and the empty tomb.

Your line: her story too. Today, read one story of a woman in the Bible, Hagar, Ruth, Mary Magdalene or Phebe, and notice what she does, not only what's done to her. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christians study the women of the Bible in reading groups and sermon series, and feminist and womanist theology is taught in some seminaries; churches differ on whether women are ordained.

fork.setup: you're Hagar, alone by a spring in the wilderness. the angel of the Lord has just spoken to you by name. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Hagar names the God who spoke to her: "Thou God seest me." the outcast in the wilderness is the one who names God.

original.note: Hebrew, Genesis 16:13: a God of seeing. Hagar's name for God; the King James renders it "Thou God seest me."

trapdoor: what you thought: a modern agenda laid over the Bible.
what it means: reading slowly to find the women already there: Hagar, the women at the cross, Mary Magdalene, Phebe.
what a scholar hears: womanist readings like Delores Williams's Hagar: God meets the outcast in the wilderness and helps her survive.

notes: Names given as examples without dates or titles: Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, Rosemary Radford Ruether, Delores Williams. 'Womanist' attributed to a word used by Alice Walker. Confirm.
Delores Williams's reading of Hagar (survival and quality of life rather than immediate liberation) is paraphrased; confirm.
Genesis 16: the hook says Hagar 'runs' after being 'treated harshly' (KJV 'dealt hardly with her'); the child-survival theme draws also on Genesis 21. Confirm the blend is fair.
Original: אֵל רֳאִי (El Roi), Genesis 16:13; confirm pointing and the note's rendering 'a God of seeing'.
Women's ordination: described as a difference between churches without ranking; confirm the wording is fair to Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant positions.
Editor pass: fixed the garbled 'the Bible turns up a lot'; cut 'waiting for someone to read slowly' (implied earlier readers missed it) and the repeated 'this path ranks none of them'.
'Phebe' is the KJV spelling (Phoebe in many modern versions).
Audit (2026-10-02): 'sent into the wilderness' and the child's survival come from Genesis 21, not 16; Genesis 21:9–19 added to sources.
